newsitem.title: CHINA: China revolutionaries and technocrats mourn Deng.
newsitem.headline: China revolutionaries and technocrats mourn Deng.

text.p: Beijing on Tuesday draped the interior of the Great Hall of the People in black banners of mourning for Deng Xiaoping, a leader grieved both by China's ageing revolutionaries and its new ruling technocrats.

In high-collared Mao suits, military uniforms and sharp western business attire, 10,000 members of China's elderly old guard and new political elite gathered for three final bows of respect to the man who transformed the nation.

Beneath a huge photograph of a smiling, avuncular Deng, President Jiang Zemin sobbed as he began a eulogy vowing to fulfil his mentor's plans for building China into an economic powerhouse under Communist Party control.
The memorial ceremony, televised live across the nation and around the world, marked official China's last farewell to Deng, who died last Wednesday aged 92 after ruling for 18 years.

While in some areas Beijing's busy streets emptied as people stopped to watch the sombre service, the traffic around the Great Hall did not miss a beat and the sounding of factory sirens and train horns to mourn Deng went unheard.
"I think that Deng was a great man," said one student hurrying to get to a television set. "Without him, China would not have the same position in the world it has now."

The official mourners gathered in the Great Hall's cavernous main auditorium in rows behind China's top leaders, who lined up before a flower-bedecked stage where Deng's ashes lay in a small box covered with the red banner of communism.

Black banners with white Chinese characters proclaimed both their grief for the past and their plans for the future, wishing "Eternal Glory to Comrade Xiaoping" and vowing unity under the new leadership of Jiang Zemin.

Jiang set the tone with his eulogy, his voice cracking theatrically with emotion as he reviewed Deng's life as a revolutionary fighter who eventually changed the lives of 1.2 billion people with capitalist-style economic reform.

The guests, most of whom remained standing throughout Jiang's hour-long speech, included most of the tiny handful of Deng's revolutionary peers who have outlived him -- stooped, elderly Communist veterans bidding goodbye to one of their own.

Also present were younger officials, whose dark western business suits marked them as part of the new order led by Jiang Zemin. The People's Liberation Army, always an important factor in China's delicate political balance, was represented by ranks of generals in full dress uniforms.

Deng's widow, Zhuo Lin, his grown children and grandchildren received grim condolences from the guests after the eulogy. Zhuo, her white hair clipped short, looked frail as she grasped a cane and was seated for much of the ceremony.

Across the city at Beijing University, seedbed of the student-led 1989 Tiananmen Square pro-democracy movement that was crushed by the army at Deng's behest, students gathered in their department lecture halls to watch the rites, with many saying they felt only sorrow at the leader's death.

"I don't hold any feelings against him because of 1989," one computer science student said. "I think at the time he made the right decision. Otherwise China might have fallen apart like the Soviet Union."

But a Beijing resident on Tiananmen Square called for an accounting of the killing of hundreds in the June 4, 1989 crackdown -- drawing a parallel with the fate of Hua Guofeng, who succeeded late Chairman Mao Zedong in 1976 only to be toppled by Deng just two years later.
"If Jiang Zemin fails to re-evaluate June 4, he will be the second Hua Guofeng," he said.
